title: Want what happens
hookLine: Epictetus: wish things to happen as they do, and life will go well (Enchiridion 8)
last: KOSMOPOLITĒS — A BIGGER HOME AROUND THE SMALLER ONE.

cards: It's raining on the day of the picnic. The flight is delayed three hours. The recipe you've made twenty times comes out flat.
The usual move is to argue with it. This shouldn't be happening. It was supposed to be sunny.

It's not fair. And the arguing goes on for an hour after the rain has soaked the sandwiches. The Stoics thought the arguing hurts more than the rain, and proposed something that sounds almost impossible.
Don't just put up with what happens. Want it.

teach.b: Start with a surprise about the word. Amor fati is Latin for love of fate, and it sounds like an ancient Stoic motto. It isn't.
No Stoic on record used the phrase. It comes from the German philosopher Friedrich Nietzsche, in the 1880s, who wanted to love everything that happens, not just bear it.
But the idea is much older, and Epictetus put it plainly in his Handbook.

teach.h: WISH THINGS TO BE AS THEY ARE.
teach.b: In George Long's translation: "Seek not that the things which happen should happen as you wish; but wish the things which happen to be as they are, and you will have a tranquil flow of life."
Flip the direction of the wish. The early Stoics had a picture for it, reported by a later writer.
A dog is tied to a moving cart. If it wants to go where the cart goes, it trots along, freely. If not, it gets dragged anyway.

Same road, different trip. Seneca, putting verses by the Stoic Cleanthes into Latin, ends them with one line: the fates lead the willing and drag the unwilling. Now the honest part, so this doesn't turn into giving up.
Remember the dichotomy of control from the weeks of practices: some things are up to us, some aren't. Amor fati is for the second column. If the rain is falling, want the rain.
But if you can fix the leak, fix the leak.

teach.h: ONLY FOR WHAT ISN'T UP TO US.
teach.b: Wanting what happens isn't pretending you don't care.
It's refusing to spend your life arguing with what already is, so your strength goes to what's still yours to do.

how: Stoic practitioners try to meet events outside their control with acceptance, even welcome, while still acting on what is up to them.

o: giving up on changing anything in your life
believing your future is fixed by the stars
wanting what happens, not just putting up with it

games.q: want what happens — tap the pairs.
p: wish things to be as they are

s: amor fati is an ancient Stoic motto
the phrase is Nietzsche's; the idea is older, in Epictetus and others.
accepting what happens means not fixing anything
acceptance is for what isn't up to us; fix the leak if you can.
Seneca wrote that the fates lead the willing and drag the unwilling
it closes his Latin version of verses by the Stoic Cleanthes.

games.q: you're a dog tied to a moving cart. what's your best move?
o: trot along where the cart goes.
games.why: the Stoic picture: same road either way, but the willing dog travels freely and the unwilling one is dragged.

practice: Bring to mind one thing today that didn't go your way and can't be changed now, and check whether some part of you is still arguing with it.
Try the flip, silently, as an experiment: all right, this is how it went; then, if you can manage it, i'll take it. Breathe with that, and see what loosens.

wordCard.voice: Amor fati. Latin for love of fate: Nietzsche's phrase for an old Stoic idea, wanting what happens instead of arguing with it.

orig.note: Latin: love of fate; Nietzsche's phrase, not an ancient one.

carryVoice: Your line: love what happens. The willing dog and the dragged one travel the same road. Day two hundred ninety-three, and counting.

sources.q: Seek not that the things which happen should happen as you wish; but wish the things which happen to be as they are, and you will have a tranquil flow of life.

sources.ref: Hippolytus, Refutation 1.21 (the dog and the cart, Zeno and Chrysippus)
